## Methods

Mouse strains and cell lines
Wild-type CD45.2 C57BL/6J (JAX stock #000664) mice were originally obtained from the Jackson Laboratory. Aiolos-deficient mice were originally obtained from Riken BRC (stock # RBRC05582) and backcrossed onto the CD45.2 C57BL/6J background for more than 10 generations to obtain CD45.2 Aiolos-deficient (Ikzf3-/-) mice. Cd8-/- mice (JAX stock #002665) were generously provided by Dr. Ginny Bumgardner and Dr. Hazem Ghoneim at The Ohio State University. All mice were housed in a specific-pathogen free (SPF) facility. Mice were housed in 12/12 dark/light cycle, at an ambient temperature of 68–79F with 29–33% humidity. Age- and sex-matched mice were used for both in vivo and in vitro studies to avoid any unintentional bias. Littermates were used wherever possible for experiments. The experimental and control animals were housed separately for the duration of the study. WT and Ikzf3-/- mice used in the study had similar starting weights for infection experiments. All studies performed utilizing mice were done with the approval of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at The Ohio State University in Columbus, OH. The EL4 murine T cell lymphoma line (TIB-39) for transfection studies and YAC-1 cells (TIB-160) for cytotoxicity were acquired from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) and maintained in complete RPMI (RPMI media [catalog # 61870-036, Thermo Fisher Scientific] containing 10% FBS [catalog # 26140-079, Life Technologies] and 1% penicillin/streptomycin [catalog # 15140-122, Life Technologies]). For transduction studies, the Platinum-E (Plat-E) Retroviral Packaging cell Line (RV-101, Cell Biolabs, Inc.) was maintained in complete DMEM (DMEM [catalog # 11995-065, Thermo Fisher Scientific], 10% FBS, and 1% penicillin/streptomycin). MDCK (Madin–Darby canine kidney cells) cell line (ATCC, NBL-2) for viral titer determination was maintained in complete RPMI (RPMI, 10mM HEPES [catalog # 15630080, Thermo Fisher Scientific], 1X L-glutamine [catalog # 25030081, Thermo Fisher Scientific], 1X sodium pyruvate [catalog # 11360070, Thermo Fisher Scientific], 1X MEM NEAA [catalog # 11140050, Thermo Fisher Scientific], 10% FBS and 1% penicillin/streptomycin).

CD8+ T cell isolation and culture
For overexpression studies, naive CD8+ T cells were isolated from the spleens and lymph nodes of 5–8-week-old Ikzf3-/- mice using the BioLegend MojoSort naive CD8+ T cell isolation kit (catalog # 480044) according to the manufacturer’s recommendations. Naive CD8+ T cells (6×105) in complete IMDM (IMDM [catalog # 12440061, Life Technologies] with 10% FBS, 1% penicillin/streptomycin, and 0.05% (50μM) 2-mercaptoethanol [catalog # M3148, Sigma-Aldrich]) were plated in wells coated with anti-CD3 (5μg/mL, clone 145-2C11, catalog # BDB553057, BD Biosciences) and anti-CD28 (10μg/mL, clone 37.51, catalog # BDB553294, BD Biosciences) in the presence of IL-4-neutralizing antibody (5μg/mL, clone 11B11, catalog # 504122, BioLegend) and IL-2-neutralizing antibody (5μg/mL, JES6-1A12, catalog # 503706, BioLegend). IL-15 complex (IL-15C) was added to the samples at a concentration of 100ng/mL of IL-15. The IL-15C was generated as previously described58. Briefly, soluble recombinant IL-15 (catalog # 447-ML-010, R&D) and recombinant mouse IL-15Rα Fc chimera (catalog # 551-MR-100, R&D) were mixed at a 1:2 ratio and incubated at 37°C for 45 min immediately prior to use. Cells were cultured in a 37°C incubator for the indicated times before downstream analyses.

Primary T cell transduction
Aiolos overexpression experiments in primary CD8+ T cells were performed as previously described26. Briefly, pMIG-Aiolos was generated by cloning the Aiolos (Ikzf3) coding sequence into the pMSCV-IRES–GFP II (pMIG II, catalog # 52107, Addgene) vector backbone. The cloning of Aiolos was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, and overexpression was validated via both qRT-PCR and immunoblot using anti-V5 antibody for Aiolos (clone SV5-Pk1; 1:20,000; catalog # R960-25, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Plat-E cells were used to package pMIG-Aiolos virus per the manufacturer’s instructions. Viral supernatants were collected 48h post-transfection and snap frozen. Viral supernatants were thawed immediately before use and added to murine CD8+ T cells, as detailed above, in the presence of polybrene (8μg/mL, catalog # 107689, Sigma Aldrich). Transduction was performed at 24 and 48h after plating CD8+ T cells via spinfection for 2h at 800xg at room temperature. At 48h, cells were treated with anti-IL-2 and IL-15C and harvested 24h after the second round of transduction for analysis.

Assessment of cytokine response and cytotoxic capacity
For functional assessment of T cells, CD8+ T cells were isolated from the spleens of 5–8-week-old WT and Ikzf3-/- mice. Cells were purified using BioLegend MojoSort CD8+ T cell isolation kit (catalog # 480035) according to the manufacturer’s recommendations. Cells were then treated with rmIL-12 (10ng/mL, catalog # 419-ML-010, R&D), rmIL-18 (10ng/mL, catalog # 9139-IL-010, R&D), and IL-15C (100ng/mL) for 30min to determine phosphorylation of STAT5 and STAT4 or for 16h to determine the production of IFN-γ and granzyme B, along with NKG2D expression. To preserve the phosphorylation of STAT proteins, cells were immediately fixed with 4% formaldehyde (37% formaldehyde, catalog # BP531, Fisher Scientific) post-stimulation and harvested for further analysis. For IFN-γ and granzyme B, cells were treated with protein transport inhibitors (PTI, catalog # 00-4980-93, Invitrogen) 4h prior to harvest for downstream analysis.

To determine T cytotoxic potential, cells were incubated with the cytokine mix as above and were co-cultured with YAC-1 cells (50,000) labeled with carboxyfluorescein succinimidyl ester (CFSE, 1μM; catalog # C34554, Thermo Fisher) at an effector-to-target (E:T) ratio of 10:1 for 6h at 37°C. Cells were then stained with the ghost viability dye (Red 780; 1:750; catalog # 13-0865-T100, Tonbo Biosciences) to determine % of dead target YAC-1 cells. The ratio of target cells killed/T was calculated as the number of dead cells in cytokine treated samples—untreated samples (background)/number of T cells. For NKG2D blocking, cells were treated with anti-NKG2D antibody (10μg/mL, clone: HMG2D; catalog # BE0111, BioXCell) or isotype control (catalog # BE0091, BioXCell) for 30min prior to YAC-1 cells addition.

Promoter-reporter assay
To generate the Eomes (pGL3-Eomes) and Il2rb (pGL3-Il2rb) promoter-reporter constructs, the regulatory region of the Eomes gene (~2kb upstream of the transcriptional start site [TSS], Primers: Forward: 5′–GATCGGTACCGGCTTCGCTGCATCAAAAC–3′, Reverse: 5′–GATCGAGCTCGCTTTAGCGAATCGCAGACG –3′), and Il2rb gene (~805bp proximal to the TSS, Primers: Forward: 5′–GATCGGTACCGGTGATGGGAAAAGAAGGGGCC –3′, Reverse: 5′–GATCACGCGTCACTCAGATCAACCACCACCTG–3′) were respectively cloned into the Promega pGL3-Promoter vector (catalog # PAE1761, Promega). Expression vectors for Aiolos, Aiolos DNA-binding mutant (AiolosDBM), and a constitutively active form of STAT5b (STAT5bCA) were generated as previously described26,59. Briefly, the coding sequence of Aiolos was cloned into the pcDNA3.1/V5-His-TOPO vector (catalog # K4800, Life Technologies). The coding sequence was confirmed by Sanger sequencing with T7 and BGH primers and then transferred into the pEF1/V5-His vector (catalog # V920-20, Life Technologies). A similar technique was utilized for the generation of AiolosDBM and STAT5bCA in conjunction with the Agilent QuikChange Site-Directed Mutagenesis kit (catalog # 200519). For AiolosDBM, point mutations were introduced into the first and second N-terminal zinc finger domains. For STAT5bCA, point mutations were introduced into STAT5b (H298R and S715F), resulting in constitutive phosphorylation of the Y699 residue. Using the Lonza 4D nucleofection system (program CM-120, buffer SF), EL4 T cells were nucleofected with the indicated vectors (V5-tagged Aiolos constructs, STAT5bCA, or empty vector control), along with pGL3-Eomes or pGL3-Il2rb and a SV40-Renilla vector as a control for transfection efficiency. Following 22–24h of recovery, samples were harvested, and luciferase expression was analyzed using the Dual-Luciferase Reporter Assay System (catalog # E1910, Promega) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Overexpression of the vectors was confirmed by Immunoblot analysis using an antibody against the V5 epitope tag (clone SV5-Pk1; 1:20,000; catalog # R960-25, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for Aiolos vectors and anti-STAT5b antibody (clone G-2; 1:10000; catalog # sc-1656, Santa Cruz Biotechnology) for STAT5bCA.

RNA-Seq analysis
CD8+ T cells were isolated from the spleens of WT and Ikzf3-/- mice as described above. Cells were then stained for CD44 (V450; 1:300; clone IM7; catalog # 560452, BD Biosciences), CD62L (APCe780; 1:300; clone MEL-14; catalog # 47-0621-82, Thermo Fisher), CD49d (AF488; 1:100; clone R1-2; catalog # 103611, BioLegend) and viability dye (V510; 1:400; catalog # 13-0870-T100, Tonbo Biosciences) to identify T populations, and were sorted using the Sony MA900 cell sorter for RNA extraction. For naive RNA samples, CD8+ T cells from the spleens of WT mice were isolated using the BioLegend MojoSort naive CD8+ T cell isolation kit as mentioned above. RNA was isolated from the sorted WT and Aiolos-deficient T cells, as well as WT naive CD8+ T cell, s using the Machery-Nagel Nucleospin RNA kit (catalog # 740955.5) as per the manufacturer’s instructions. Purified RNA samples were submitted to Azenta Life Sciences for polyA selection, library preparation, and Illumina 2×150bp sequencing.

Data were pre-processed with Trimmomatic (0.36) and aligned with STAR (2.5.2b) to GRCm38. Transcript counts were generated with Subread (1.5.2) and quantified with DESeq2 (v1.44.0) for analysis. Before analysis, expression data were filtered to exclude non-protein coding transcripts and lowly expressed genes (less than 100 counts). Genes with a DESeq2 adjusted p<0.05 were considered differentially expressed. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) plots were generated with DESeq2 and exported to GraphPad Prism for visualization. Morpheus software (https://software.broadinstitute.org/morpheus) was used for heatmap generation and clustering by Euclidean distance using normalized log2 counts from DESeq2 analysis. Volcano plot was generated using −log10 (adjusted p value) and log2 fold change values from DESeq2 analysis in the VolcaNoseR software (https://huygens.science.uva.nl/VolcaNoseR/)60. For gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), differentially expressed genes were pre-ranked by multiplying the sign of the fold-change by −log10 (adjusted p value) and analyzed using the Broad Institute GSEA software (v 4.3.3) for comparison against “gene ontology,” and “immunologic signature” gene sets.

ATAC-seq analysis
WT and Ikzf3-/- splenic T cells were isolated as described above. ATAC-seq analysis was performed as previously described61. Briefly, 5×104 cells at >90% viability were processed using the Illumina-compatible Tn5 Transposase (catalog # C01070012-30), followed by a cleanup using the Qiagen MinElute PCR Purification Kit (catalog # 28004) prior to amplification with NEBNext® High-Fidelity 2X PCR Master Mix (catalog # M0541S) and Illumina primers, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Purified DNA were submitted to CD Genomics for sequencing by Illumina Novaseq X. Resultant sequences were trimmed and aligned to mm10 using Bowtie 2 (v2.5.1), then processed with SAMtools (v1.21) and converted to bigwigs with deepTools (v3.5.6). Peaks were overlapped with ENCODE regulatory elements, and counts at peaks were determined using deepTools. Regions with adjusted P values <0.05 were considered statistically significant. PCA, significant peaks, and data for heatmaps were generated with DESeq2. PCA values were exported to prism for visualization. Heatmap generation and hierarchical clustering of the regions with significant differential accessibility was performed using the Morpheus software (https://software.broadinstitute.org/morpheus). Volcano plot was generated using log10 (adjusted p value) and log2 fold change values in the VolcaNoseR software (https://huygens.science.uva.nl/VolcaNoseR/)60. CPM-normalized tracks were visualized using Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV, v2.18.2).

Influenza A virus infection and tissue preparation
IAV strain A/PR/8/34 (H1N1, termed “PR8”) was propagated in 10-day-old specific pathogen free embryonated chicken eggs (Charles River Laboratories) and titered on MDCK cells (BEI Resources, NIAID, NIH: Kidney [Canine], NR-2628). WT and Aiolos-deficient mice between 8–12 weeks of age were infected intranasally with 30 or 100 plaque-forming units (PFU) of IAV. For the adoptive transfer studies, WT and Ikzf3-/- T cells were sorted as described above and retro-orbitally transferred into recipient Cd8-/- mice. The recipient mice were then infected via the intranasal route with 100 PFU of IAV. At designated times after infection, spleen and lung tissues were harvested following euthanasia with CO2 inhalation as previously described26. To distinguish circulating from resident cells, mice were retro-orbitally injected with fluorophore-labeled anti-CD45.2 antibody (PE-anti CD45.2, 2μg, clone # 104, catalog # 109808, BioLegend) 3min prior to euthanasia14.

For spleen, mediastinal lymph nodes, and thymus, single-cell suspensions were generated in tissue processing media (IMDM+4% FBS) by passing the tissue through a 100µm nylon mesh strainer followed by erythrocyte lysis in 0.84% NH4Cl. For lungs, the whole tissue was incubated in HBSS (catalog # 14175103, Gibco) with 1.3mM EDTA. Lung as well as liver tissues were dissociated in Collagenase IV (catalog # LS004189, Worthington Biochemical) supplemented media (RPMI+4% FBS) using a gentleMACS Dissociator (Miltenyi Biotech) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Samples were then filtered through a 40μm nylon mesh strainer and layered with a Percoll (catalog # 17-0891-01, Sigma) density gradient to isolate lymphocytes. Cells were centrifuged at 500×g for 20min with brakes off to allow for separation of mononuclear cells. Cells were then collected, and erythrocyte lysis was performed as previously described. Blood was collected into tubes containing 4% sodium citrate solution, and Ficoll (catalog # 17144003, Cytiva) was added for density separation. Cells were centrifuged as above with brakes off to allow mononuclear cell separation. Cells were resuspended in FACS buffer (PBS [catalog # 14190-136, Thermo Fisher Scientific] + 4% FBS) prior to staining for flow cytometry.

FTY720 administration
Mice were injected with saline control or Fingolimod (FTY720, catalog # S5002, Selleckchem) at 1mg/kg in saline daily via the intraperitoneal route at the indicated time points. Tissues were then collected post-euthanasia at the indicated times for processing and analysis.

Flow cytometry
For flow cytometry analysis, cells were first incubated with anti-mouse CD16/32 Fc block (clone 93; catalog # 101320; BioLegend) for 5min at 4°C. Cells were then incubated for 30min at 4°C for extracellular staining with following antibodies: anti-CD8α (BV570, 1:300; clone 53-6.7; catalog # 100740, BioLegend), anti-CD3 (BV605; 1:100; clone 17A2; catalog # 100237, BioLegend), anti-CD44 (BV785; 1:300; clone IM7; catalog # 103059, BioLegend), anti-CD62L (BV650; 1:300; clone MEL-14; catalog # 104453, BioLegend), anti-CD49d (BUV395; 1:100; clone R1-2; catalog # 740219, BD Biosciences), anti-CD122 (FITC/APC; 1:00; clone 5H4; catalog # 554452, BD Biosciences/105912, BioLegend), anti-Cxcr3 (BV750; 1:100; clone CXCR3-173; catalog # 747298, BD Biosciences), anti-NKG2D (PE-Dazzle 594; 1:100; clone CX5; catalog # 130214, BioLegend) and Ghost viability dye (Red 780; 1:750; catalog # 13-0865-T100, Tonbo Biosciences). Cells were then washed twice with FACS buffer prior to intracellular staining. For intracellular staining, cells were fixed and permeabilized using the eBioscience Foxp3 transcription factor staining kit (catalog # 00-5523-00, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 30min or overnight at 4°C. After fixation, samples were stained with the following antibodies in 1X permeabilization buffer (catalog # 00-5523-00, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 30min at room temperature: anti-Aiolos (PE/AF647; 1:100; clone S48-791; catalog # 564874/565265, BD Biosciences), anti-Eomes (PE-Cy7; 1:100; clone DAN11MAG; catalog # 25-4875-82, Thermo Fisher Scientific), anti-T-bet (PerCP-Cy5.5; 1:100; clone 4B10; catalog # 644806, BioLegend) anti-IFN-γ (APC; 1:500; clone XMG1.2; catalog # 505810, BioLegend) and anti-granzyme B (PE; 1:250; clone GB11; catalog # GRB04, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were then washed with 1X permeabilization buffer and FACS buffer before resuspending in FACS buffer for analysis. To determine the phosphorylation levels of STAT proteins, cells were immediately fixed with 4% formaldehyde post-stimulation to preserve the phosphorylation of STAT proteins. Cells were then harvested and washed with 1X PBS prior to incubation with anti-CD49d (AF488) and anti-CD44 (V450) antibodies for 30min at 4°C. Following the extracellular staining, cells were permeabilized with cold methanol overnight at −20°C. These cells were then incubated with antibodies against pY-STAT5 (Y694, APC; 1:12.5; clone: SRBCZX; catalog # 17901042, Fisher Scientific), pY-STAT4 (PY933, PerCP-Cy5.5; 1:12.5; clone: 38/p-Stat4; catalog # 561217, BD Biosciences), and CD8α (PE, 1:300; clone 53-6.7; catalog # 100708, BioLegend), for 30min before resuspending in FACS buffer for analysis. Samples were run on a BD FACSCanto II or BD FACS Symphony and analyzed using FlowJo software (version 10.8.1).

Virus titers and viral RNA determination
Virus titers and virus RNA were determined as previously described62–64. Briefly, mice were euthanized at designated time points post-infection, and lungs were harvested in 1mL PBS+0.5% BSA in Precellys tubes (catalog # 50-154-2932, Bertin Corp) for homogenization using the Precellys homogenizer. The lung supernatants were collected, snap frozen, and stored at −80°C prior to use. For the determination of virus titers, MDCK cells were plated at a density of 7×105 cells/well in a 6-well plate. Virus supernatants were 10-fold serially diluted and added to MDCK cells in the presence of infection media (1X PBS, 35% BSA [catalog # ICN810061, Fisher Scientific], 1X Ca/Mg). Following 1h incubation at 37°C the the viral supernatant was removed, and cells were washed with 1X PBS. An overlay (2% Oxoid agar [catalog # LP0028, Thermo Fisher Scientific], 2X MEM [catalog # 12-684F, Lonza], TPCK Trypsin [catalog # 20233, Thermo Fisher Scientific], DEAE-Dextran [catalog # MP 021951331, Thermo Fisher Scientific], 5% sodium bicarbonate, and H2O) was added to the wells. After 48h of incubation, the overlay was removed, and cells were fixed with 3% paraformaldehyde (PFA). Cells were blocked with 5% non-fat milk in 1X PBS and incubated with chicken anti-PR8 antibody (catalog # NR-3098, BEI Resources) and rabbit anti-chicken peroxidase (catalog # 303-035-003, Jackson ImmunoResearch). The number of plaques formed were quantified following the addition of TrueBlue Peroxidase (catalog # KPL5510-0030, Thermo Fisher Scientific).

For viral RNA determination, lungs were harvested in 1mL Trizol (catalog # 15596026, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and processed as above. 1-bromo-3-chloropropane (catalog # B62404, Sigma Aldrich) was added to the clarified virus supernatant. The aqueous layer was collected post-centrifugation, ethanol was added, and the mixture was transferred onto a spin column from the Machery-Nagel Nucleospin RNA kit. RNA was extracted according to the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA was prepared, and qRT-PCR analysis was then performed to determine virus RNA levels.

## Paper

## Abstract

CD8+ virtual memory T (T ) cells rapidly respond to infection via antigen-independent bystander effector functions. While it is recognized that T cells arise independently of foreign antigen encounter, the mechanisms governing their development are not fully understood. Here, we identify the Ikaros transcription factor Aiolos as a negative regulator of T cell programming. We observe enhanced frequencies and numbers of T in the spleen, liver, and blood of unchallenged Aiolos-deficient (Ikzf3-/-) mice and in the lungs 1-day post-infection with influenza A virus (IAV). Furthermore, Ikzf3-/- T cells produce elevated IFN-γ and granzyme B in response to cytokine stimulation. Importantly, Aiolos-deficient mice control IAV more rapidly and exhibit reduced morbidity, indicating enhanced T cell functionality. Mechanistically, Aiolos represses the expression of the transcription factor Eomes and the IL-15R subunit CD122, known positive regulators of T gene program. Collectively, these findings establish Aiolos as a molecular repressor of T programming and responses.

---

## Introduction

Host infection results in the generation of diverse, antigen-specific CD8+ memory T cell populations that persist long-term to safeguard against re-infection1–4. These include central memory T (T ), effector memory T (T ), and tissue-resident memory T (T ) cell subsets, among others, which are distinguished by their functional properties, including the ability to recirculate or reside in peripheral tissues1,5,6. In contrast to these antigen-specific populations, a more recently described subset, termed virtual memory T (T ) cells, arises independently of foreign antigen encounter7–9. As T and T cells both express L-selectin (CD62L) and the activation marker CD44, T were previously categorized as a part of the T repertoire. However, recent findings have established that low surface expression of the integrin receptor CD49d, an indicator of foreign antigen-encounter, distinguishes T (CD62L+CD44+CD49dLo) from these other T cell populations10,11. As T cell generation is not dependent upon foreign antigen exposure, they are found in significant numbers in uninfected and unchallenged hosts8. During infection, T cells rapidly infiltrate affected sites and provide bystander protection independent of TCR engagement7,10,12,13. As such, these cells comprise a critical component of the first line of defense against various pathogenic infections14–16.

T effector responses are driven by signals from cytokines such as IL-12, IL-18, and IL-15 and include the production of additional inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IFN-γ) and NKG2D-mediated bystander cytotoxicity7,10,13. T cells can also differentiate into antigen-specific effector and memory T cell subsets, as their polyclonal repertoire allows for clonal expansion7,11,14,17. In addition to infection, T have also been shown to infiltrate tumors and target cancer cells independent of MHC-I18,19. Despite having a high avidity for self-antigen, which could be a concern for autoimmunity, these cells demonstrate high self-tolerance and promote homeostasis20,21. Together, their rapid, antigen-independent responses and ability to differentiate in an antigen-specific manner make T cells a uniquely versatile T cell population and notable therapeutic target for the treatment of a range of diseases.

T development and function are dependent upon signals from the cytokine IL-15, as IL-15-deficient mice (IL-15-/-) lack T cells7,12. The response to IL-15 in T cells is mediated by signals received through the shared receptor subunit CD122 (IL-15Rβ/IL-2Rβ)7. Expression of CD122 is positively regulated by the T-box transcription factor Eomesodermin (Eomes), which is highly expressed in T cells and is essential for their differentiation and survival7,19. While Eomes promotes CD122 expression, IL-15 signaling in turn induces Eomes expression in CD8+ T cells12,22. However, the identity of the upstream regulators of this critical regulatory loop, as well as the comprehensive mechanisms underlying T effector functions, remain unknown.

Here, we identify Aiolos as a repressor of T cell differentiation and function. We find that Aiolos-deficient (Ikzf3-/-) mice have significantly elevated frequencies and numbers of T cells both in secondary lymphoid organs at steady-state, and in the lungs 24h following IAV infection. We further find that Aiolos-deficient T have elevated expression of Eomes and enhanced effector functions in response to cytokine stimulation. Importantly, this results in enhanced viral control and reduced morbidity of IAV-infected Aiolos-deficient mice relative to wild-type (WT). Collectively, these findings highlight Aiolos as a negative regulator of T cell formation and functional responses, suggesting that Aiolos could have therapeutic potential in enhancing antiviral immunity.

---

## Results

Aiolos suppresses Eomes and CD122 expression in CD8+ T cells
Eomes is a key regulator of CD8+ T cell differentiation and effector programs and is essential for T formation23–25. We previously established that loss of Aiolos in effector CD4+ T cells during IAV infection (A/PR/8/34 (H1N1), termed “PR8”) results in augmented expression of the transcription factor Eomes and induction of a cytotoxic gene program26. As such, we sought to determine whether the relationship between Aiolos and Eomes may be a conserved feature in CD8+ T cells and whether this may impact the generation of T .

Initially, we examined Eomes protein expression in CD8+ T cells isolated from the spleens of unchallenged, specific-pathogen free (SPF) WT and Aiolos-deficient mice. Aiolos-deficient mice had elevated frequencies and numbers of Eomes+ T cells, and an overall increase in the abundance of Eomes protein expression compared to WT controls (Fig. 1a–c). Further analysis of CD8+ T cells revealed increased percentages of Eomes+ naive (CD62L+CD44-) and activated (CD44+) T cells in Aiolos-deficient mice compared to WT (Supplementary Fig. 1a–d). Aiolos deficiency similarly impacted the expression of the IL-15R subunit CD122, an Eomes target gene encoded by Il2rb (Fig. 1d, e)25. To further define the role of Aiolos in regulating Eomes and CD122 expression, we overexpressed Aiolos in Ikzf3-/- CD8+ T cells using retroviral transduction (Supplementary Fig. 2a, b). Overexpression of Aiolos resulted in a significant decrease in the expression of both Eomes and CD122 (Supplementary Fig. 2c, d). Collectively, these in vivo and in vitro data demonstrate that Aiolos represses Eomes and CD122 expression in primary CD8+ T cells.

To determine the mechanism by which Aiolos suppresses Eomes and CD122, we analyzed publicly available Aiolos ChIP-Seq data from murine thymocytes [GSM510606527]. Analysis of Aiolos enrichment across the Eomes and Il2rb genes using Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) revealed peaks proximal to the Eomes and Il2rb promoter regions, suggesting that Aiolos may directly repress their expression (Fig. 1f, Supplementary Fig. 2e). To assess potential impacts of Aiolos, we generated plasmids to overexpress Aiolos or an Aiolos DNA-binding mutant (AiolosDBM), along with gene reporter constructs containing the identified Eomes or Il2rb regulatory regions. Aiolos overexpression resulted in suppression of both Eomes and Il2rb gene-reporter activity (Fig. 1g, Supplementary Fig. 2f). However, the repressive effect was lost with the AiolosDBM mutant, indicating that direct DNA binding is necessary for the repressive effect of Aiolos (Fig. 1g, Supplementary Fig. 2f). A known driver of Eomes expression in CD8+ T cells is the transcription factor STAT528. Interestingly, sites of STAT5b enrichment [GSM788751229] at the Eomes promoter region overlapped with the Aiolos enrichment sites (Fig. 1f). This is in line with previously published studies indicating that IkZF and STAT factor DNA-binding motifs overlap26,30,31. To determine whether Aiolos may repress Eomes expression by interfering with STAT5 mediated induction of Eomes, we overexpressed a constitutively active form of STAT5b (STAT5bCA) along with Aiolos in EL4 T cells. As expected, STAT5b overexpression alone significantly enhanced Eomes promoter activity. However, co-expression with Aiolos abrogated the STAT5-induced response (Fig. 1h). Together, these findings support Aiolos as a transcriptional repressor of Eomes in CD8+ T cells through direct interaction or via competition with STAT5 for promoter occupancy. Further, our data also support Aiolos-dependent suppression of CD122 in these cells, which could result in their decreased responsiveness to IL-15. Given the interplay between IL-15 signaling and Eomes, these findings are suggestive of a mechanism whereby Aiolos represses the IL-15/STAT5/Eomes regulatory axis and potentially T differentiation.

Aiolos expression inversely correlates with that of Eomes and CD122 in T cells
We next assessed the expression of Aiolos, Eomes, and CD122 in splenic CD8+ T naive, effector (T , CD62L-CD44+), and T cells. To distinguish between circulating (CD45.2(i.v.Pos)) and non-circulating resident cells, we retro-orbitally injected mice with fluorophore-labeled anti-CD45.2 antibody prior to euthanasia (Supplementary Fig. 3a). Analysis of the resident (CD45.2(i.v.Neg)) CD8+ T cell populations revealed increased expression of Eomes and CD122 in T cells relative to T cells, while Aiolos expression exhibited the opposite trend (Supplementary Fig. 3b, c). This inverse correlation between Aiolos expression and that of both Eomes and CD122 supports a role for Aiolos in negatively regulating T formation.

Aiolos deficiency results in an expanded T population
We next sought to determine the impact of Aiolos deficiency on T cell generation. We began by assessing T cell populations in the spleens of unchallenged, SPF WT, and Aiolos-deficient mice7,9. We observed no differences in CD3+ T cells, a slight reduction in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, and a slight increase in double negative (DN) T cells in the spleen of Aiolos-deficient mice compared to WT, consistent with findings in human patients and mouse models harboring Aiolos variants and genetic mutations (Supplementary Fig. 4a, b)27,32–37. Further characterization of both CD4 and CD8 T cells revealed decreased naive cells with an increased effector population in the absence of Aiolos (Supplementary Fig. 4c, d), again in line with observations in human patients with Aiolos variants27,32–37. However, in the CD8+ T cell population, we observed a difference in the CD62L+CD44+ subset in which there was a substantial increase in Aiolos-deficient mice (Supplementary Fig. 4c, d). As it has been reported that T cells make up the majority of CD62L+CD44+ population in the uninfected host, we next used CD49d expression to distinguish T from T cells10,14,38. Consistent with elevated Eomes and CD122 expression (Fig. 1a–e), we observed a significant increase in both the frequency and numbers of T cells in the spleens of Aiolos-deficient mice compared to WT (Fig. 2a, b). We next examined T populations in the blood, liver, and mediastinal lymph nodes and found similar increases in both frequency and numbers of T in Aiolos-deficient mice compared to WT (Fig. 2c, d). In contrast to the aforementioned tissues, few T were found in the lungs of either WT or Aiolos-deficient mice (Fig. 2d). We also noted that Aiolos-deficient T from these tissues exhibited elevated expression of both Eomes and CD122 relative to WT (Fig. 2e, f, Supplementary Fig. 5a, b).

T cells form in the periphery; however, we considered the possibility that Aiolos may impact their cellular precursors in the thymus7,8,12,38. As such, we next examined thymic CD8+ T cells in WT and Aiolos-deficient mice. Consistent with published results, we observed no difference in the frequency of CD8+ T cells between WT and Aiolos-deficient samples (Supplementary Fig. 5c)36. Notably, frequencies of CD8+ Eomes+ and CD8+ CD122+ were relatively low in the thymus of both WT and Aiolos-deficient mice. There was no difference in the frequency and number of CD8+ Eomes+ T cells, and only a slight increase in frequency, but not numbers, of CD8+ CD122+ cells in the absence of Aiolos (Supplementary Fig. 5d, e). Taken together, these findings support a role for Aiolos in repressing T cell programming, at least in part, through modulation of Eomes and IL-15 responsiveness in the periphery.

Aiolos deficiency promotes T gene programming
To assess potential broader impacts of Aiolos on T programming, we performed RNA-sequencing analysis of T cells isolated from the spleens of unchallenged WT and Aiolos-deficient mice, in comparison to WT naive CD8+ T cells as a control. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of transcripts for T cells and WT naive CD8+ T cells revealed distinct clusters between the naive and T samples, as has been previously reported7. Importantly, PCA analysis of the T transcripts revealed that Aiolos-deficient T samples formed a cluster distinct from WT T (Supplementary Fig. 6a). Hierarchical clustering of the top 200 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) identified unique gene expression patterns between WT and Aiolos-deficient T cells (Supplementary Fig. 6b). In Aiolos-deficient T cells, genes involved in T transcriptional regulation (Eomes, Tbx21) were upregulated along with cytokine receptors known to promote T homeostasis and responsiveness to IL-15 (Il15ra, Il2rb) (Fig. 3a, b)7,12. In addition, genes involved in T cell migration into infected tissues (Ccr2, Cxcr3, S1pr5) were upregulated in the absence of Aiolos, whereas genes encoding residency markers (Itgae, Cd69) were downregulated in Aiolos-deficient T samples (Fig. 3a, b)7,14. We subsequently validated the protein expression for T-bet (Tbx21) and the chemokine receptor CXCR3 (Cxcr3) in naive CD8+ T and T cells14,25. As expected, we observed increased expression of these factors in T cells compared to the naive counterparts. Importantly, their expression was significantly higher in Aiolos-deficient T cells when compared to WT T , corroborating our findings from the RNA-seq analysis (Fig. 3c, d).

In addition to increased tissue infiltration, CCR2-expressing T cells are reported to exhibit enhanced effector responses compared to the CCR2-deficient T cells14. Indeed, analysis of the transcript data revealed that Aiolos-deficient T exhibited increased expression of natural killer cell-associated (Klrk1, Klrc1, Klra4, and Klra8), cytolytic (Gzma, Gzmb, Prf1, Fasl), and cytokine (Ifng) genes (Fig. 3a, b)9,39,40. Further, GSEA analysis of gene ontology and immunologic signature subsets suggested that genes involved in IL-15 signaling, innate immune responses, and effector and memory responses were upregulated in Aiolos-deficient T cells (Fig. 3e, f, Supplementary Fig. 6c–e). Collectively, these data suggest that T may have enhanced effector responses in the absence of Aiolos.

Aiolos alters chromatin accessibility at regulatory regions for T genes
To determine whether Aiolos impacts the T gene program through alterations in chromatin accessibility, we next performed Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin (ATAC)-seq analysis on T cells isolated from the spleens of WT and Aiolos-deficient mice. Similar to RNA-Seq data, PCA analysis revealed distinct genotype clusters with broad changes in the chromatin accessibility between WT and Aiolos-deficient T samples, with the majority of gene regulatory regions displaying increased accessibility (Supplementary Fig. 7a, b). Consistent with the RNA-seq data, there was increased accessibility at the regulatory regions of key T transcription factors (Eomes, Tbx21), cytokine receptors (Il2rb, Il12rb2, Il18r1), chemokine receptors (Ccr2, Ccr5, Cxcr3), and effector molecules (Ifng, Gzmb, Prf1, Klrk1) in the absence of Aiolos (Fig. 4a–f, Supplementary Fig. 7c–f). In contrast, chromatin accessibility was reduced at the regulatory regions of other genes involved in cytokine responses (Ifngr1, Ifngr2, Tgfbr2), tissue-residency (Itgae, Cd69), and migration (Ccr9, Cxcr5) (Fig. 4a, b, Supplementary Fig. 7g, h). These findings suggest that Aiolos governs T gene programming directly and/or indirectly through alterations in chromatin accessibility at key regulatory and effector genes.

Aiolos deficiency enhances the functional capacity of T cells
One of the functional characteristics of T cells is to provide rapid bystander protection through the production of molecules like IFN-γ, granzyme B, and NKG2D in response to cytokine stimulation (IL-12, IL-18, and IL-15)7,10. We hypothesized that the absence of Aiolos may augment responsiveness to these cytokines via alterations in cytokine receptor subunit expression. Indeed, genes encoding IL-15R subunits (Il15ra, Il2rb), IL-12R subunits (Il12rb1, Il12rb2), and IL-18R subunits (Il18r1 and Il18rap) were upregulated in T cells in the absence of Aiolos, suggesting that Aiolos deficiency may selectively augment T responsiveness to these cytokines (Figs. 3b and 5a). GSEA analysis of the immunologic signatures also revealed that genes related to IL-15/STAT5 and IL-12/STAT4 signaling were upregulated in Aiolos-deficient T cells (Fig. 3e, Supplementary Fig. 6e). To determine whether increased expression of cytokine receptor subunits resulted in a functional difference in cytokine signaling, we assessed the tyrosine phosphorylation status of STAT5 (pY-STAT5) and STAT4 (pY-STAT4) in T cells exposed to a cytokine cocktail (IL-12, IL-18, and IL-15C) ex vivo (Fig. 5b). Indeed, we observed increases in both pY-STAT5 and pY-STAT4 in the Aiolos-deficient T cells compared to WT, suggestive of an enhanced cytokine responsiveness in the absence of Aiolos (Fig. 5c, d, Supplementary Fig. 8a, b). To assess whether increased cytokine signaling had a functional consequence, we examined production of IFN-γ and GzmB and found that Aiolos-deficient T cells produced significantly elevated levels of IFN-γ and GzmB compared to WT (Fig. 5e, f, Supplementary Fig. 8c, d). We similarly examined the expression of NKG2D (encoded by Klrk1), which allows for the innate-like bystander cytotoxic functions of T cells38,41. Again, we observed increased frequency and expression of NKG2D in Aiolos-deficient T cells compared to WT in response to cytokine treatment (Fig. 5g, Supplementary Fig. 8e). We next performed a cytotoxicity assay and found increased killing of target YAC-1 cells by Aiolos-deficient T cells in the presence of stimulating cytokines compared to WT (Fig. 5h, Supplementary Fig. 8f)7,11,42. Notably, blocking NKG2D resulted in a significant reduction in target cell killing, specifically by Aiolos-deficient cells (Fig. 5h). Collectively, these data demonstrate that T have enhanced effector responses in the absence of Aiolos.

Aiolos deficiency results in increased control of IAV infection
To determine the impact of Aiolos on T responses in vivo, we next infected WT and Ikzf3-/- mice with IAV (Supplementary Fig. 9a). Through the course of infection, animal body weights were measured daily as an assessment of infection progression and disease severity. Consistent with past observations, Aiolos-deficient mice exhibited significantly less weight loss compared to WT mice, with differences observed as early as 5 d.p.i. (Supplementary Fig. 9b)26. To determine whether the reduced weight loss was an outcome of reduced viral burden in the absence of Aiolos, we assessed viral load in the lung homogenates at 3 d.p.i. Indeed, both viral RNA and infectious virus titers were significantly reduced in Aiolos-deficient mice relative to WT, suggesting a level of increased antiviral response in the absence of Aiolos (Supplementary Fig. 9c). As Aiolos expression is largely restricted to cells of the lymphoid lineage, these early differences suggest an impact of Aiolos on an early-responding lymphocyte subset, perhaps T 43.

Aiolos deficiency enhances the response of CD8+ T cells to IAV infection
Qian and colleagues demonstrated that T cells can be found in IAV-infected lungs as early as 1-day post-infection (1 d.p.i.)14. To determine whether the absence of Aiolos would augment this response, we infected WT and Aiolos-deficient mice with IAV and assessed T populations at 1 d.p.i. Similar to our observations in uninfected mice, the frequency and number of T cells were increased in the spleen of Aiolos-deficient mice at 1 d.p.i. compared to WT (Fig. 6a, b). Strikingly, there was also a substantial increase in the number of resident CD8+ T cells in the lungs of Aiolos-deficient mice compared to WT (Fig. 6c–e). Consistent with our previous findings, Aiolos-deficient T cells from infected spleens and lungs exhibited elevated expression of both Eomes and CD122 at 1 d.p.i. compared to WT (Supplementary Fig. 10a, b).

Comparative analysis of T cells in the spleens and lungs of WT and Ikzf3-/- mice revealed an average 2-fold increase in the number of T cells of Aiolos-deficient mice compared to WT. However, there was an approximate 12-fold average increase in the number of T cells in the lungs of these mice compared to WT, suggesting baseline differences in T numbers in Aiolos-deficient animals is not sufficient to account for this increase in the lungs (Fig. 6f). To determine whether the increased lung T population had trafficked from outside the lungs or rather had expanded from a lung-resident population, we treated WT and Ikzf3-/- mice with Fingolimod (FTY720) or saline control via the intraperitoneal route daily starting 1 day prior to IAV infection (Fig. 6g). FTY720 suppresses lymphocyte migration and has been widely used to study CD8+ T cell egress to infected tissues44,45. Following FTY720 administration, we infected mice with IAV and examined the presence of resident CD8+ T cells in the lungs at 3 d.p.i. As before, infected animals treated with saline control displayed a significant increase in resident CD8+ T cells in the lungs of Aiolos-deficient mice relative to WT. In contrast, FTY720-treated animals had diminished resident CD8+ T cell populations in the lungs of both WT and Aiolos-deficient mice, indicating that T cells migrated to the lungs in response to infection and that this migration was enhanced in the absence of Aiolos (Fig. 6h).

Early lung-infiltrating Aiolos-deficient T correlate with enhanced control of IAV
To determine whether Aiolos-deficient T harbored an enhanced capacity to combat infection, we initially infected WT and Ikzf3-/- mice with IAV, followed by FTY720 administration from 1 to 5 d.p.i to limit our analyses to the impact of early-responding T (Fig. 7a). Consistent with our previous findings (Supplementary Fig. 9b), Aiolos-deficient animals lost significantly less weight than their WT counterparts, with differences observed as early as 3 d.p.i (Fig. 7b). In fact, Aiolos-deficient mice lost very little weight throughout the 6-day time course. Analysis of the lungs at 3 and 6 d.p.i revealed increased resident CD8+ T cells in the lungs of Aiolos-deficient mice compared to WT, and an assessment of viral RNA at day 3 revealed significantly reduced levels in the lungs of FTY720-treated Aiolos-deficient mice compared to WT (Fig. 7c, d). Notably, there was no difference in viral RNA levels between saline control and FTY720-treated mice at day 3, despite reduced numbers of resident CD8+ T cells in FTY720-treated mice compared to controls (Supplementary Fig. 11a, b). By 6 d.p.i., viral RNA levels were comparable between WT and Aiolos-deficient mice (Fig. 7d). However, there was no difference between the viral RNA present in Aiolos-deficient mice at 3 and 6 d.p.i., again suggesting more rapid control of the virus in these animals relative to WT (Fig. 7d).

To further assess the enhanced protective capacity of Aiolos-deficient T cells, we adoptively transferred WT or Ikzf3-/- CD8+ T cells into recipient Cd8-/- mice and infected recipients with IAV 1-day post-transfer (Fig. 7e). We then measured viral RNA levels in the lungs of the recipient mice at 3 d.p.i. Consistent with our prior findings, we observed reduced viral RNA in the lungs of mice that received Aiolos-deficient T compared to mice that received WT T cells (Fig. 7f). Together, these findings demonstrate that Aiolos-deficient T have an enhanced capacity to control IAV infection relative to their WT counterparts.

## Methods

Mouse strains and cell lines
Wild-type CD45.2 C57BL/6J (JAX stock #000664) mice were originally obtained from the Jackson Laboratory. Aiolos-deficient mice were originally obtained from Riken BRC (stock # RBRC05582) and backcrossed onto the CD45.2 C57BL/6J background for more than 10 generations to obtain CD45.2 Aiolos-deficient (Ikzf3-/-) mice. Cd8-/- mice (JAX stock #002665) were generously provided by Dr. Ginny Bumgardner and Dr. Hazem Ghoneim at The Ohio State University. All mice were housed in a specific-pathogen free (SPF) facility. Mice were housed in 12/12 dark/light cycle, at an ambient temperature of 68–79F with 29–33% humidity. Age- and sex-matched mice were used for both in vivo and in vitro studies to avoid any unintentional bias. Littermates were used wherever possible for experiments. The experimental and control animals were housed separately for the duration of the study. WT and Ikzf3-/- mice used in the study had similar starting weights for infection experiments. All studies performed utilizing mice were done with the approval of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at The Ohio State University in Columbus, OH. The EL4 murine T cell lymphoma line (TIB-39) for transfection studies and YAC-1 cells (TIB-160) for cytotoxicity were acquired from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) and maintained in complete RPMI (RPMI media [catalog # 61870-036, Thermo Fisher Scientific] containing 10% FBS [catalog # 26140-079, Life Technologies] and 1% penicillin/streptomycin [catalog # 15140-122, Life Technologies]). For transduction studies, the Platinum-E (Plat-E) Retroviral Packaging cell Line (RV-101, Cell Biolabs, Inc.) was maintained in complete DMEM (DMEM [catalog # 11995-065, Thermo Fisher Scientific], 10% FBS, and 1% penicillin/streptomycin). MDCK (Madin–Darby canine kidney cells) cell line (ATCC, NBL-2) for viral titer determination was maintained in complete RPMI (RPMI, 10mM HEPES [catalog # 15630080, Thermo Fisher Scientific], 1X L-glutamine [catalog # 25030081, Thermo Fisher Scientific], 1X sodium pyruvate [catalog # 11360070, Thermo Fisher Scientific], 1X MEM NEAA [catalog # 11140050, Thermo Fisher Scientific], 10% FBS and 1% penicillin/streptomycin).

CD8+ T cell isolation and culture
For overexpression studies, naive CD8+ T cells were isolated from the spleens and lymph nodes of 5–8-week-old Ikzf3-/- mice using the BioLegend MojoSort naive CD8+ T cell isolation kit (catalog # 480044) according to the manufacturer’s recommendations. Naive CD8+ T cells (6×105) in complete IMDM (IMDM [catalog # 12440061, Life Technologies] with 10% FBS, 1% penicillin/streptomycin, and 0.05% (50μM) 2-mercaptoethanol [catalog # M3148, Sigma-Aldrich]) were plated in wells coated with anti-CD3 (5μg/mL, clone 145-2C11, catalog # BDB553057, BD Biosciences) and anti-CD28 (10μg/mL, clone 37.51, catalog # BDB553294, BD Biosciences) in the presence of IL-4-neutralizing antibody (5μg/mL, clone 11B11, catalog # 504122, BioLegend) and IL-2-neutralizing antibody (5μg/mL, JES6-1A12, catalog # 503706, BioLegend). IL-15 complex (IL-15C) was added to the samples at a concentration of 100ng/mL of IL-15. The IL-15C was generated as previously described58. Briefly, soluble recombinant IL-15 (catalog # 447-ML-010, R&D) and recombinant mouse IL-15Rα Fc chimera (catalog # 551-MR-100, R&D) were mixed at a 1:2 ratio and incubated at 37°C for 45 min immediately prior to use. Cells were cultured in a 37°C incubator for the indicated times before downstream analyses.

Primary T cell transduction
Aiolos overexpression experiments in primary CD8+ T cells were performed as previously described26. Briefly, pMIG-Aiolos was generated by cloning the Aiolos (Ikzf3) coding sequence into the pMSCV-IRES–GFP II (pMIG II, catalog # 52107, Addgene) vector backbone. The cloning of Aiolos was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, and overexpression was validated via both qRT-PCR and immunoblot using anti-V5 antibody for Aiolos (clone SV5-Pk1; 1:20,000; catalog # R960-25, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Plat-E cells were used to package pMIG-Aiolos virus per the manufacturer’s instructions. Viral supernatants were collected 48h post-transfection and snap frozen. Viral supernatants were thawed immediately before use and added to murine CD8+ T cells, as detailed above, in the presence of polybrene (8μg/mL, catalog # 107689, Sigma Aldrich). Transduction was performed at 24 and 48h after plating CD8+ T cells via spinfection for 2h at 800xg at room temperature. At 48h, cells were treated with anti-IL-2 and IL-15C and harvested 24h after the second round of transduction for analysis.

Assessment of cytokine response and cytotoxic capacity
For functional assessment of T cells, CD8+ T cells were isolated from the spleens of 5–8-week-old WT and Ikzf3-/- mice. Cells were purified using BioLegend MojoSort CD8+ T cell isolation kit (catalog # 480035) according to the manufacturer’s recommendations. Cells were then treated with rmIL-12 (10ng/mL, catalog # 419-ML-010, R&D), rmIL-18 (10ng/mL, catalog # 9139-IL-010, R&D), and IL-15C (100ng/mL) for 30min to determine phosphorylation of STAT5 and STAT4 or for 16h to determine the production of IFN-γ and granzyme B, along with NKG2D expression. To preserve the phosphorylation of STAT proteins, cells were immediately fixed with 4% formaldehyde (37% formaldehyde, catalog # BP531, Fisher Scientific) post-stimulation and harvested for further analysis. For IFN-γ and granzyme B, cells were treated with protein transport inhibitors (PTI, catalog # 00-4980-93, Invitrogen) 4h prior to harvest for downstream analysis.

To determine T cytotoxic potential, cells were incubated with the cytokine mix as above and were co-cultured with YAC-1 cells (50,000) labeled with carboxyfluorescein succinimidyl ester (CFSE, 1μM; catalog # C34554, Thermo Fisher) at an effector-to-target (E:T) ratio of 10:1 for 6h at 37°C. Cells were then stained with the ghost viability dye (Red 780; 1:750; catalog # 13-0865-T100, Tonbo Biosciences) to determine % of dead target YAC-1 cells. The ratio of target cells killed/T was calculated as the number of dead cells in cytokine treated samples—untreated samples (background)/number of T cells. For NKG2D blocking, cells were treated with anti-NKG2D antibody (10μg/mL, clone: HMG2D; catalog # BE0111, BioXCell) or isotype control (catalog # BE0091, BioXCell) for 30min prior to YAC-1 cells addition.

Promoter-reporter assay
To generate the Eomes (pGL3-Eomes) and Il2rb (pGL3-Il2rb) promoter-reporter constructs, the regulatory region of the Eomes gene (~2kb upstream of the transcriptional start site [TSS], Primers: Forward: 5′–GATCGGTACCGGCTTCGCTGCATCAAAAC–3′, Reverse: 5′–GATCGAGCTCGCTTTAGCGAATCGCAGACG –3′), and Il2rb gene (~805bp proximal to the TSS, Primers: Forward: 5′–GATCGGTACCGGTGATGGGAAAAGAAGGGGCC –3′, Reverse: 5′–GATCACGCGTCACTCAGATCAACCACCACCTG–3′) were respectively cloned into the Promega pGL3-Promoter vector (catalog # PAE1761, Promega). Expression vectors for Aiolos, Aiolos DNA-binding mutant (AiolosDBM), and a constitutively active form of STAT5b (STAT5bCA) were generated as previously described26,59. Briefly, the coding sequence of Aiolos was cloned into the pcDNA3.1/V5-His-TOPO vector (catalog # K4800, Life Technologies). The coding sequence was confirmed by Sanger sequencing with T7 and BGH primers and then transferred into the pEF1/V5-His vector (catalog # V920-20, Life Technologies). A similar technique was utilized for the generation of AiolosDBM and STAT5bCA in conjunction with the Agilent QuikChange Site-Directed Mutagenesis kit (catalog # 200519). For AiolosDBM, point mutations were introduced into the first and second N-terminal zinc finger domains. For STAT5bCA, point mutations were introduced into STAT5b (H298R and S715F), resulting in constitutive phosphorylation of the Y699 residue. Using the Lonza 4D nucleofection system (program CM-120, buffer SF), EL4 T cells were nucleofected with the indicated vectors (V5-tagged Aiolos constructs, STAT5bCA, or empty vector control), along with pGL3-Eomes or pGL3-Il2rb and a SV40-Renilla vector as a control for transfection efficiency. Following 22–24h of recovery, samples were harvested, and luciferase expression was analyzed using the Dual-Luciferase Reporter Assay System (catalog # E1910, Promega) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Overexpression of the vectors was confirmed by Immunoblot analysis using an antibody against the V5 epitope tag (clone SV5-Pk1; 1:20,000; catalog # R960-25, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for Aiolos vectors and anti-STAT5b antibody (clone G-2; 1:10000; catalog # sc-1656, Santa Cruz Biotechnology) for STAT5bCA.

RNA-Seq analysis
CD8+ T cells were isolated from the spleens of WT and Ikzf3-/- mice as described above. Cells were then stained for CD44 (V450; 1:300; clone IM7; catalog # 560452, BD Biosciences), CD62L (APCe780; 1:300; clone MEL-14; catalog # 47-0621-82, Thermo Fisher), CD49d (AF488; 1:100; clone R1-2; catalog # 103611, BioLegend) and viability dye (V510; 1:400; catalog # 13-0870-T100, Tonbo Biosciences) to identify T populations, and were sorted using the Sony MA900 cell sorter for RNA extraction. For naive RNA samples, CD8+ T cells from the spleens of WT mice were isolated using the BioLegend MojoSort naive CD8+ T cell isolation kit as mentioned above. RNA was isolated from the sorted WT and Aiolos-deficient T cells, as well as WT naive CD8+ T cell, s using the Machery-Nagel Nucleospin RNA kit (catalog # 740955.5) as per the manufacturer’s instructions. Purified RNA samples were submitted to Azenta Life Sciences for polyA selection, library preparation, and Illumina 2×150bp sequencing.

Data were pre-processed with Trimmomatic (0.36) and aligned with STAR (2.5.2b) to GRCm38. Transcript counts were generated with Subread (1.5.2) and quantified with DESeq2 (v1.44.0) for analysis. Before analysis, expression data were filtered to exclude non-protein coding transcripts and lowly expressed genes (less than 100 counts). Genes with a DESeq2 adjusted p<0.05 were considered differentially expressed. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) plots were generated with DESeq2 and exported to GraphPad Prism for visualization. Morpheus software (https://software.broadinstitute.org/morpheus) was used for heatmap generation and clustering by Euclidean distance using normalized log2 counts from DESeq2 analysis. Volcano plot was generated using −log10 (adjusted p value) and log2 fold change values from DESeq2 analysis in the VolcaNoseR software (https://huygens.science.uva.nl/VolcaNoseR/)60. For gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), differentially expressed genes were pre-ranked by multiplying the sign of the fold-change by −log10 (adjusted p value) and analyzed using the Broad Institute GSEA software (v 4.3.3) for comparison against “gene ontology,” and “immunologic signature” gene sets.

ATAC-seq analysis
WT and Ikzf3-/- splenic T cells were isolated as described above. ATAC-seq analysis was performed as previously described61. Briefly, 5×104 cells at >90% viability were processed using the Illumina-compatible Tn5 Transposase (catalog # C01070012-30), followed by a cleanup using the Qiagen MinElute PCR Purification Kit (catalog # 28004) prior to amplification with NEBNext® High-Fidelity 2X PCR Master Mix (catalog # M0541S) and Illumina primers, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Purified DNA were submitted to CD Genomics for sequencing by Illumina Novaseq X. Resultant sequences were trimmed and aligned to mm10 using Bowtie 2 (v2.5.1), then processed with SAMtools (v1.21) and converted to bigwigs with deepTools (v3.5.6). Peaks were overlapped with ENCODE regulatory elements, and counts at peaks were determined using deepTools. Regions with adjusted P values <0.05 were considered statistically significant. PCA, significant peaks, and data for heatmaps were generated with DESeq2. PCA values were exported to prism for visualization. Heatmap generation and hierarchical clustering of the regions with significant differential accessibility was performed using the Morpheus software (https://software.broadinstitute.org/morpheus). Volcano plot was generated using log10 (adjusted p value) and log2 fold change values in the VolcaNoseR software (https://huygens.science.uva.nl/VolcaNoseR/)60. CPM-normalized tracks were visualized using Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV, v2.18.2).

Influenza A virus infection and tissue preparation
IAV strain A/PR/8/34 (H1N1, termed “PR8”) was propagated in 10-day-old specific pathogen free embryonated chicken eggs (Charles River Laboratories) and titered on MDCK cells (BEI Resources, NIAID, NIH: Kidney [Canine], NR-2628). WT and Aiolos-deficient mice between 8–12 weeks of age were infected intranasally with 30 or 100 plaque-forming units (PFU) of IAV. For the adoptive transfer studies, WT and Ikzf3-/- T cells were sorted as described above and retro-orbitally transferred into recipient Cd8-/- mice. The recipient mice were then infected via the intranasal route with 100 PFU of IAV. At designated times after infection, spleen and lung tissues were harvested following euthanasia with CO2 inhalation as previously described26. To distinguish circulating from resident cells, mice were retro-orbitally injected with fluorophore-labeled anti-CD45.2 antibody (PE-anti CD45.2, 2μg, clone # 104, catalog # 109808, BioLegend) 3min prior to euthanasia14.

For spleen, mediastinal lymph nodes, and thymus, single-cell suspensions were generated in tissue processing media (IMDM+4% FBS) by passing the tissue through a 100µm nylon mesh strainer followed by erythrocyte lysis in 0.84% NH4Cl. For lungs, the whole tissue was incubated in HBSS (catalog # 14175103, Gibco) with 1.3mM EDTA. Lung as well as liver tissues were dissociated in Collagenase IV (catalog # LS004189, Worthington Biochemical) supplemented media (RPMI+4% FBS) using a gentleMACS Dissociator (Miltenyi Biotech) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Samples were then filtered through a 40μm nylon mesh strainer and layered with a Percoll (catalog # 17-0891-01, Sigma) density gradient to isolate lymphocytes. Cells were centrifuged at 500×g for 20min with brakes off to allow for separation of mononuclear cells. Cells were then collected, and erythrocyte lysis was performed as previously described. Blood was collected into tubes containing 4% sodium citrate solution, and Ficoll (catalog # 17144003, Cytiva) was added for density separation. Cells were centrifuged as above with brakes off to allow mononuclear cell separation. Cells were resuspended in FACS buffer (PBS [catalog # 14190-136, Thermo Fisher Scientific] + 4% FBS) prior to staining for flow cytometry.

FTY720 administration
Mice were injected with saline control or Fingolimod (FTY720, catalog # S5002, Selleckchem) at 1mg/kg in saline daily via the intraperitoneal route at the indicated time points. Tissues were then collected post-euthanasia at the indicated times for processing and analysis.

Flow cytometry
For flow cytometry analysis, cells were first incubated with anti-mouse CD16/32 Fc block (clone 93; catalog # 101320; BioLegend) for 5min at 4°C. Cells were then incubated for 30min at 4°C for extracellular staining with following antibodies: anti-CD8α (BV570, 1:300; clone 53-6.7; catalog # 100740, BioLegend), anti-CD3 (BV605; 1:100; clone 17A2; catalog # 100237, BioLegend), anti-CD44 (BV785; 1:300; clone IM7; catalog # 103059, BioLegend), anti-CD62L (BV650; 1:300; clone MEL-14; catalog # 104453, BioLegend), anti-CD49d (BUV395; 1:100; clone R1-2; catalog # 740219, BD Biosciences), anti-CD122 (FITC/APC; 1:00; clone 5H4; catalog # 554452, BD Biosciences/105912, BioLegend), anti-Cxcr3 (BV750; 1:100; clone CXCR3-173; catalog # 747298, BD Biosciences), anti-NKG2D (PE-Dazzle 594; 1:100; clone CX5; catalog # 130214, BioLegend) and Ghost viability dye (Red 780; 1:750; catalog # 13-0865-T100, Tonbo Biosciences). Cells were then washed twice with FACS buffer prior to intracellular staining. For intracellular staining, cells were fixed and permeabilized using the eBioscience Foxp3 transcription factor staining kit (catalog # 00-5523-00, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 30min or overnight at 4°C. After fixation, samples were stained with the following antibodies in 1X permeabilization buffer (catalog # 00-5523-00, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 30min at room temperature: anti-Aiolos (PE/AF647; 1:100; clone S48-791; catalog # 564874/565265, BD Biosciences), anti-Eomes (PE-Cy7; 1:100; clone DAN11MAG; catalog # 25-4875-82, Thermo Fisher Scientific), anti-T-bet (PerCP-Cy5.5; 1:100; clone 4B10; catalog # 644806, BioLegend) anti-IFN-γ (APC; 1:500; clone XMG1.2; catalog # 505810, BioLegend) and anti-granzyme B (PE; 1:250; clone GB11; catalog # GRB04, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were then washed with 1X permeabilization buffer and FACS buffer before resuspending in FACS buffer for analysis. To determine the phosphorylation levels of STAT proteins, cells were immediately fixed with 4% formaldehyde post-stimulation to preserve the phosphorylation of STAT proteins. Cells were then harvested and washed with 1X PBS prior to incubation with anti-CD49d (AF488) and anti-CD44 (V450) antibodies for 30min at 4°C. Following the extracellular staining, cells were permeabilized with cold methanol overnight at −20°C. These cells were then incubated with antibodies against pY-STAT5 (Y694, APC; 1:12.5; clone: SRBCZX; catalog # 17901042, Fisher Scientific), pY-STAT4 (PY933, PerCP-Cy5.5; 1:12.5; clone: 38/p-Stat4; catalog # 561217, BD Biosciences), and CD8α (PE, 1:300; clone 53-6.7; catalog # 100708, BioLegend), for 30min before resuspending in FACS buffer for analysis. Samples were run on a BD FACSCanto II or BD FACS Symphony and analyzed using FlowJo software (version 10.8.1).

Virus titers and viral RNA determination
Virus titers and virus RNA were determined as previously described62–64. Briefly, mice were euthanized at designated time points post-infection, and lungs were harvested in 1mL PBS+0.5% BSA in Precellys tubes (catalog # 50-154-2932, Bertin Corp) for homogenization using the Precellys homogenizer. The lung supernatants were collected, snap frozen, and stored at −80°C prior to use. For the determination of virus titers, MDCK cells were plated at a density of 7×105 cells/well in a 6-well plate. Virus supernatants were 10-fold serially diluted and added to MDCK cells in the presence of infection media (1X PBS, 35% BSA [catalog # ICN810061, Fisher Scientific], 1X Ca/Mg). Following 1h incubation at 37°C the the viral supernatant was removed, and cells were washed with 1X PBS. An overlay (2% Oxoid agar [catalog # LP0028, Thermo Fisher Scientific], 2X MEM [catalog # 12-684F, Lonza], TPCK Trypsin [catalog # 20233, Thermo Fisher Scientific], DEAE-Dextran [catalog # MP 021951331, Thermo Fisher Scientific], 5% sodium bicarbonate, and H2O) was added to the wells. After 48h of incubation, the overlay was removed, and cells were fixed with 3% paraformaldehyde (PFA). Cells were blocked with 5% non-fat milk in 1X PBS and incubated with chicken anti-PR8 antibody (catalog # NR-3098, BEI Resources) and rabbit anti-chicken peroxidase (catalog # 303-035-003, Jackson ImmunoResearch). The number of plaques formed were quantified following the addition of TrueBlue Peroxidase (catalog # KPL5510-0030, Thermo Fisher Scientific).

For viral RNA determination, lungs were harvested in 1mL Trizol (catalog # 15596026, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and processed as above. 1-bromo-3-chloropropane (catalog # B62404, Sigma Aldrich) was added to the clarified virus supernatant. The aqueous layer was collected post-centrifugation, ethanol was added, and the mixture was transferred onto a spin column from the Machery-Nagel Nucleospin RNA kit. RNA was extracted according to the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA was prepared, and qRT-PCR analysis was then performed to determine virus RNA levels.

RNA isolation and Quantitative Real-Time PCR
RNA was isolated as described above utilizing the Machery-Nagel Nucleospin RNA kit per the manufacturer’s guidelines. cDNA was then generated using the Superscript IV First Strand Synthesis System (catalog # 18091050, Thermo Fisher Scientific). SYBR Select Mastermix for CFX (catalog # 4472942, ThermoFisher) was used for qRT-PCR reactions with 10ng cDNA per reaction on the CFX Connect (Bio Rad). The following primers were used: (IAV NP primers- Forward: 5′ –GATTGGTGGAATTGGACGAT–3′, Reverse: 5′ –AGAGCACCATTCTCTCTATT – 3′, Rps18 primers- Forward: 5′ –GGAGAACTCACGGAGGATGAG–3′, Reverse: 5′ –CGCAGCTTGTTGTCTAGACCG-3′). Outputs were normalized to Rps18 and are presented as relative to their respective control, as indicated.

Immunoblot analysis
For immunoblot analysis, cells were harvested, lysed in 1X SDS loading dye, (50mM Tris [pH 6.8], 100mM DTT, 2% SDS, 0.1% bromophenol blue, 10% glycerol), and boiled for 15min. Lysates were separated via SDS-PAGE on 10% Bis-Tris Bolt gels (catalog # NW00102BOX, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and then transferred onto a 0.45µm nitrocellulose membrane (catalog # 10600002, Cytiva). Membranes were blocked with 2% nonfat dry milk in 1X TBST (10mM Tris [pH 8.0], 150mM NaCl, 0.05% Tween-20). Membranes were then incubated with the following antibodies to detect proteins: α-V5 (1:20,000; clone SV5-Pk1, catalog # R960-25, Thermo Fisher Scientific), α-STAT5b antibody (1:10,000; clone G-2, catalog # sc-1656, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), goat α-mouse HRP (1:10,000; catalog # 115-035-174, Jackson Immunoresearch), α-β-actin-HRP (1:15,000; clone: 2D1D10, catalog # A00730, GenScript). Clarity Max Western ECL substrate (catalog # 1705062, BioRad) was used for the visualization of protein bands.

Statistics and reproducibility
All statistical analyses were performed using the GraphPad Prism software (version 10.3.1). Unpaired Student’s t-test was performed for single comparisons. For multiple comparisons, one-way or two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparisons test were performed, as appropriate. Error bars indicate the standard error of the mean. P values ≤0.05 were considered statistically significant. DESeq2 was used for RNA- and ATAC-seq analysis.

### Reviewer 1

This study by by Pokhrei S and the colleagues demonstrates the crucial role of the transcription factor Ikzf3 in the
development and function of virtual memory T (Tvm) cells. Given that the mechanisms underlying Tvm cell development and
functional acquisition remain largely unexplored, this research contributes significantly to advancing our understanding of

the expression of Eomes and CD122 also increase in Tvm cells in other organs such as lymph nodes, liver, and lungs in

in Figure 2c and 2d, a comparison with true memory CD8⁺ T cells induced by vaccination or infection would strengthen the

capture the dynamics of viral clearance and immune response.
5. In Figure 7, was there any difference in survival rate between WT and Ikzf3⁻/⁻ mice?

### Reviewer 3

CD8 Virtual Memory T cells are memory-like CD8 T cells that are rapidly recruited to site of infections where they provide
antigen-independent bystander effector function such as production of inflammatory cytokines and cytotoxic factors in
response to IL12 and IL18.
CD8 TVM cells develop without encountering foreign antigens and the primary pathway for their differentiation is thought to
involve the activation of naïve CD8 T cells by cytokines such as IL-4, IL-15, and IL-7, independent of TCR signaling. It is also
suggested that a subset of CD8 T cells receiving relatively strong self-peptide-MHC signals during positive selection in the
thymus acquire TVM-like properties. However, this pathway is not considered the predominant route for TVM cell
development as most TVMs are produced in the periphery.
In this manuscript the authors address the role of the Ikaros family member Aiolos (Ikzf3) in the generation and function of
CD8+ TVM cells. They show that the number of CD8 CD62+CD44+CD49dlo TVM cells in the spleen is significantly
increased compared to WT mice in uninfected Aiolos mutant mice. Using a combination of molecular, biochemical, and
functional analyses they establish that Aiolos deficient TVM cells exhibit enhanced functionality. They show that Eomes a
key regulator of TVM function is increased in expression as are many of its downstream targets such as CD122 that
mediates IL15 signaling. Given these well documented findings it is proposed that AIOLOS modulates TVM function by
repressing the Eomes and STAT5 transcriptional networks, a very good hypothesis. However, these exciting findings need to be
further substantiated with studies on the precise role of Aiolos in CD8 TVM development and function.
There are several points to address:
a) Eomes expression is already increased in Ikzf3⁻/⁻ naïve CD8 T cells (Supplementary Figure 1a) indicating that intrinsic
differences exist at this stage and raising the possibility of changes in other cell types that may influence TVM differentiation
